title: Quartz only
hook: India winds its watches and waits months to buy one. Can a new company change what India wears on its wrist?
role: You run Titan, a new watch company, 1984 to 1993

profit.label: Sales
profit.hint: Money your watches bring in today

future.label: Lead
future.hint: How far ahead of the old watchmakers you are

intro.text: Bangalore, 1984. The Tata group and Tamil Nadu's development body have just set up a watch company, and you run it from a small room in a hotel. India makes only about 1.5 million watches a year, and HMT, the state-owned maker, makes about a million of them.

intro2.text: Watches are so hard to get that many buyers order one and wait for months, while the rich buy smuggled foreign watches. A French firm, France Ebauches, will teach your team, and a factory is going up at Hosur. Your job is to make the watches India wants before anyone else does.

d1.title: Which kind of watch?
d1.setup: It is 1985, and a new rule lets you choose your own mix of watches. Almost every watch in India is mechanical: you wind it, and it can tick for years. Quartz watches run on a battery and keep better time. HMT tried quartz in the 1970s, but those watches cost more and sold poorly.
d1.question: What will your factory make?
d1.advisor: India already knows and trusts mechanical watches. Quartz is newer and keeps changing, but it has failed here before.

options.label: Start with mechanical watches like HMT, then add quartz when buyers begin asking for it.
options.outcome: Your first watches work well, but they look and work much like HMT's, so shops ask why anyone should pay more for a new name. Your team gets good at the old craft but falls behind on the new one.
options.why: You built for the market as it was, not where it was going. Quartz was improving fast, while mechanical watches were not. Remember: judge a new thing by how fast it improves, not by how it sells today.
options.better: Make only quartz watches, so the whole factory learns the new way while HMT stays with the old one.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you followed the leader into mechanical watches. A new company can win by building for where the market is going.

options.label: Make only quartz watches, betting on a type of watch that has already failed in India once.
options.outcome: You choose quartz only. With France Ebauches teaching your team, watchmaking starts at Hosur in 1986. But the very first batch has a problem: a watch given to J.R.D. Tata, the group's chairman, does not work. Your team goes back to the bench.
options.why: Quartz kept better time, and the technology was improving fast. HMT judged it by poor sales in the 1970s and stayed with the old way. Remember: judge a new thing by how fast it improves.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you bet everything on quartz. Something that sells badly today can still become the future if it keeps getting better.

options.label: Make both mechanical and quartz watches, so one wrong bet cannot sink the company.
options.outcome: You split the factory in two. Each line is small, so each costs more to run, and your team must learn two crafts at once. The quartz watches come out later than planned.
options.why: Spreading the risk felt safer, but it split a small company's money and skills in half. Remember: judge a new thing by how fast it improves, and back it fully once you believe in it.
options.better: Put everything into quartz, so the whole team masters the new way faster than anyone else.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you split your bet between old and new. A small company that divides its effort can end up slow at both.

d2.title: Price the first watches

setup.text: It is early 1987, and your first range is ready: five collections of mechanical watches, from plain steel to gold-plated. They look better than HMT's but work the same way. HMT's watches are seen as plain, useful tools, while people with money still buy smuggled foreign ones.

It is early 1987, and your first range is ready: five collections, some mechanical and some quartz, with fewer quartz watches than you hoped for. HMT's watches are seen as plain, useful tools, while people with money still buy smuggled foreign ones.

It is early 1987, and your first range is ready: five collections, from steel to gold-plated dials with leather straps. HMT's watches are seen as plain, useful tools, while people with money still buy smuggled foreign ones.

d2.question: How do you price your first watches?
d2.advisor: Near HMT's prices, we can sell more watches, but it may be hard to earn back the factory cost. Near foreign-watch prices, far fewer people can buy.

options.label: Price close to HMT, so more families can afford one and sales can grow quickly.
options.outcome: Shops sell your watches quickly, but you earn very little on each one. Buyers start to see Titan as just another cheap watch, and money for ads and new designs runs short.
options.why: The low price made the watch feel ordinary and left little money to build the brand. Remember: price from what the buyer values, not only from your cost or your rival's price.
options.better: Price Titan as a special Indian brand: above HMT, but still within reach of a family on a salary.
options.takeaway: In 1987 you priced like the old leader. A low price can make a better product feel ordinary.

options.label: Price close to foreign watches, so Titan can feel as special as an imported watch.
options.outcome: A few rich buyers try your watches. But most people who want a smart watch cannot pay that much, while many rich buyers still prefer a foreign name.
options.why: A high price works only when buyers already believe in the name, and a new Indian brand had not earned that trust yet. Remember: price from what the buyer values.
options.better: Price Titan as a special Indian brand that a middle-class family can still save up for.
options.takeaway: In 1987 you priced like an import. A new name cannot charge for status it has not earned yet.

options.label: Price as a special Indian brand: above HMT, but still in reach of a family on a salary.
options.outcome: Your five collections go on sale at about Rs 350 to 900. That is more than people pay for a plain tool, but far less than a smuggled foreign watch. Your aim is a well-designed watch that ordinary Indians can afford.
options.why: You priced from what buyers would value: a smart watch they could be proud of, at a price a salaried family could save for. Remember: price from what the buyer values, not only from your cost.
options.takeaway: In 1987 you priced Titan above the old leader but kept it within reach. The right price tells buyers what your product is worth.

d3.title: What do your ads say?

setup.text: Your cheap watches are selling, but buyers see them as ordinary, and there is little money left for ads. HMT has long stood for tough watches that last for years. Most Indians have never thought of a watch as something stylish.
Your watches are now in shops, and people need a reason to notice them. HMT has long stood for tough watches that last for years. Most Indians have never thought of a watch as something stylish.

d3.question: What do your ads say about Titan?
d3.advisor: Buyers already trust tough watches and like a good deal. Style is newer here, so we do not know how much they will care about it.

options.label: Sell the look: show each watch big and close up, with its price beside it.
options.outcome: Your half-page newspaper ads look like a catalogue, with big, true-to-life pictures of the watches, their prices and nothing else. On TV, the ads play a tune by Mozart. Slowly, people begin to see a watch as something to show off and give as a gift.
options.why: HMT already owned toughness in buyers' minds. You gave people a different reason to want a watch: how it looks on the wrist. Remember: sell what you stand for, not just the specs.
options.takeaway: In 1987 you sold style, not toughness. People buy what a brand stands for, not only what it does.

options.label: Promise toughness: make Titan the watch that lasts for years, like the ones India already trusts.
options.outcome: Your ads promise a watch that lasts, but HMT has made that promise for years, and buyers trust HMT more. The ads leave people asking why they should switch to a new name.
options.why: You fought HMT on ground it already owned and gave buyers no new reason to choose Titan. Remember: sell what you stand for, not just the specs.
options.better: Sell something HMT does not own: style and design, with a watch to show off and give as a gift.
options.takeaway: In 1987 you copied the leader's promise. A new brand needs a reason of its own.

options.label: Promise value: show how much watch buyers get for their money, with features at every price.
options.outcome: People read the ads and agree that the watches are good value. But the ads look like everyone else's, and a week later few people remember the name.
options.why: A list of features tells people what the watch does, but it may not give them a reason to want it. Remember: sell what you stand for, not just the specs.
options.better: Sell the look with big pictures of the watches, so buyers see something they can feel proud to wear.
options.takeaway: In 1987 you sold features. Features can explain a product without making people want it.

d4.title: How will buyers find you?
d4.setup: Until now, buying a watch often meant placing an order and waiting for months. Watches reach shops through set distributors, but Titan is a new name and has no shops of its own.
d4.question: How do you get your watches to buyers?
d4.advisor: Distributors can put us in thousands of shops quickly. Building our own route will be slower and cost more.

options.label: Sell only through your own showrooms in big cities, so you control every place that sells Titan.
options.outcome: Your showrooms look smart, and the staff know every watch. But you can open only a few each year, so people in most towns still cannot find a Titan.
options.why: You built the right kind of shop, but not enough of them. Remember: build your selling around how buyers now want to shop, and reach them where they already go.
options.better: Sell straight to shop owners you choose, train their salesmen, and also open your own showroom.
options.takeaway: In 1987 you sold only through your own showrooms. Control helps, but buyers still need to be able to find you.

options.label: Skip distributors: choose shop owners, train their salesmen, and also open your own showroom.

outcome.text: You sell straight to shop owners and train salesmen to explain the watches. On 23 December 1987, your first showroom opens at Safina Plaza in Bengaluru, and people come holding pictures cut out of your ads. You sell 17 watches that day and 313 that month.

You sell straight to shop owners and train salesmen to explain the watches. In December 1987 your first showroom opens in Bengaluru, but sales start slowly because few people yet know what your watches stand for.

options.why: Buyers were used to waiting for a plain watch. Titan let them walk in, see a range and choose one that day, with someone there to explain it. Remember: build your selling around how buyers now want to shop, not how sellers always have.
options.takeaway: In 1987 you built a new way to sell a new kind of watch. A new product often needs a new road to the buyer.

options.label: Use the big distributors that already supply watch shops across India.
options.outcome: Your watches reach many shops quickly, but they sit in a drawer beside HMT's, and the staff cannot explain why yours are worth more. Sales start well, then slow down.
options.why: The old chain was built to sell the old kind of watch. A new kind needed sellers who could show it off and explain it. Remember: build your selling around how buyers now want to shop.
options.better: Sell straight to shop owners you choose, train their salesmen, and open a showroom of your own.
options.takeaway: In 1987 you sold a new watch through the old route. That route was built for the old product.

text.text: In its first year, Titan becomes India's leading maker of quartz watches with hands. In March 1988 J.R.D. Tata opens the Hosur factory, and on 10 April 1989 it makes its millionth watch. The gold-plated Classique is your best-seller, while HMT still makes mostly mechanical watches.

It is 1989. In March 1988 J.R.D. Tata opened the Hosur factory. Your quartz watches are selling, but more slowly than you hoped. HMT still makes mostly mechanical watches, so the quartz market is yours to lose.
It is 1989. The Hosur factory now makes more quartz watches, and that half of your range sells best. Your mechanical line still struggles against HMT, and you wish you had moved faster.
It is 1989. Buyers in the cities now ask for quartz watches, but your factory is still mostly mechanical. You start moving Hosur over to quartz, years behind where you could have been.

d5.title: Take on the world?

setup.text: It is 1993. Titan is India's leading maker of quartz watches, and it has sold some watches abroad since 1991. Now you want to build a name around the world. Europe is home to the Swiss, the most famous watchmakers of all.

It is 1993. Titan is still finding its feet at home, but it has sold some watches abroad since 1991. The board now wants a name around the world. Europe is home to the Swiss, the most famous watchmakers of all.

d5.question: Where do you take Titan next?
d5.advisor: Europe offers the biggest prize, but it is also the hardest market. Nearer markets are smaller and may bring less attention.

options.label: Buy a small Swiss watch brand, so Titan enters Europe with a name buyers already know.
options.outcome: The deal costs a lot, and the Swiss brand turns out to be small for a reason. Your managers fly back and forth to fix it, while the business at home gets less of their time.
options.why: You paid for someone else's name instead of growing from your own strength. Remember: choose who you serve first, and start where you are strong.
options.better: Grow first where buyers are closer to the ones you know, like the Gulf and Asia, then take on Europe later.
options.takeaway: In 1993 you bought a foreign name. You can buy a brand, but not the strength behind it.

options.label: Enter Europe under Titan's own name and compete with the Swiss in their home market.
options.outcome: In 1993 Titan goes into Europe. Shops there want strict delivery dates and top quality on every watch, and Titan struggles to keep up. In time it pulls back and focuses on India, the Middle East and the Far East.
options.why: Europe was the hardest watch market in the world, and Titan was still young. A smaller, nearer step could have taught it more at a lower cost. Remember: choose who you serve first.
options.better: Grow first in the Gulf and Asia, where buyers are nearer and more like your buyers at home. Then take on Europe later, from a stronger position.
options.takeaway: In 1993 you went straight for the hardest market. The biggest prize is not always the best first step.

options.label: Grow in the Gulf and Asia first, a smaller step that few people will notice.
options.outcome: Your watches sell in the Gulf and across Asia, where many buyers already know the name from home. These shops are easier to serve, and the money comes back to pay for new designs at Hosur.
options.why: You grew where Titan's strengths already worked and learned how to sell abroad before facing the Swiss. Remember: choose who you serve first.
options.takeaway: In 1993 you took the smaller, nearer step abroad. Win the buyers closest to you before chasing the biggest prize.

text.text: By 2012, Titan sells more than 60 of every 100 watches in India's organised watch market. HMT turned to quartz only in the early 1990s, too late, and its watch business shut in 2016. Your bet on quartz changed what India wears on its wrist.

You took a different road, but Titan still becomes the watch India is proud to wear. The old makers are slow to follow you into quartz, and by the time they do, shoppers have already chosen your name.

survivor.title: A good watch, a smaller name

text.text: Titan survives, but it spent its early years making the same kind of watch as HMT. It sells well in some cities, while other brands take the lead in quartz.
Titan survives and sells well in some cities, but it never quite becomes the name everyone wants. HMT and newer brands share the rest of the market.

collapse.title: Back to the drawing board
collapse.text: Your watches never find enough buyers. The Hosur factory runs half empty, and the Tata group starts to ask whether watches were a mistake.

fired.title: The board picks a new boss
fired.text: After three costly calls, the Tata group and its Tamil Nadu partner lose faith in you and choose someone else to run Titan.

realHistory: Titan was set up in 1984 by the Tata group and TIDCO, Tamil Nadu's development body, after years of fighting rules that kept watchmaking for the state and small firms. When a 1985 rule let it choose, it made only quartz watches, while HMT stayed mostly mechanical. Its first five collections came out in 1987 at about Rs 350 to 900, with ads that showed the watches up close with their prices. It sold directly to shop owners, trained salesmen, and opened its own showroom in Bengaluru in December 1987. It made its millionth watch in April 1989. In 1993 it went into Europe, where it struggled. In time, it pulled back to India, the Middle East and the Far East. HMT turned to quartz only in the early 1990s and kept losing ground. By 2012 Titan held over 60% of India's organised watch market, and HMT's watch unit shut in 2016.
